summary: Describes the Multicast Transport Protocol, a reliable transport that uses the multicast ability of the networks underneath it. It lets a group of receivers get the same data reliably from a sender. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1301 describes a transport protocol for groups of programs working together on the same problem. It lets them all receive the same data at once, without any of them needing to know who else is taking part, and it makes sure the data still arrives if something is lost on the way.

subtitle: A transport protocol for a group of programs that all need the same data.

tldr.problem: A group of programs collaborating over a network all need the same data, and none of them knows in advance who the others are or where they are.
tldr.mechanism: The Multicast Transport Protocol puts one member in charge, hands out permission to send one message at a time, and multicasts the data to everyone, so that receivers recover losses by asking for them rather than by each acknowledging success.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that specifies no standard, and it says so itself: security issues are not discussed in it.

today: RFC 1301 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes version 1 of MTP, a transport protocol for a group of processes collaborating over a multicast-capable network, and the security considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

sections.title: What the Multicast Transport Protocol Is For
sections.content:
RFC 1301 describes a flow controlled, atomic multicasting transport protocol, and it sets out enough information to implement it. The goal is reliable transport that uses the multicast capability of the network layers underneath. The point is to let an arbitrary number of transport providers, that is, applications, hold a real-time collaboration without any of them needing to know the population or the geographical spread of the participants. The protocol is not tied to one network architecture, but it does assume some form of multicasting or broadcasting at the data link level and some way of passing that capability up through the layers to the transport.

MTP is a transport in the OSI sense: it is a client of the network layer. It provides reliable delivery of client data between one or more communicating processes and a predefined principal process. The collection of processes is called a web. As well as moving data, MTP provides the synchronisation the members need to agree on the order in which messages are received, and to agree on whether a message was delivered even when the network is partitioned. That ordering and agreement uses serialized tokens granted by the master to the producers.

Members come in three classes, each a formal superset of the one before. A consumer can only receive user data; it may send control packets such as negative acknowledgements but may never send data. A producer may send data to the whole web as well as receive it. The master is the principal member, with all the powers of a producer and the extra duty of handing out tokens and overseeing the membership and the operating parameters. Exactly one member is the master.

One design decision shapes everything else. MTP is a negative acknowledgement protocol. It relies on the high reliability of the local and wide area networks of the day, and a receiver that gets data correctly says nothing at all. Only a loss produces a message, and those messages travel back unicast to the sender, so the reverse traffic needed to keep the web in step stays small.
sections.plainLanguage: MTP is for a group of programs that all need the same information, such as a shared whiteboard. One of them is in charge and gives each speaker permission to speak in turn, and the data goes out to everyone at once. Nobody has to keep a list of who is taking part.

sections.title: The MTP Packet Header
sections.content:
An MTP packet is a fixed transport header followed by a variable amount of data, which is either user data or extra transport information depending on the packet type. The header fields are statically defined as fixed-width quantities, there are no undefined fields, and any reserved field must always be zero.

The first byte is the protocol version, and this document describes version 1, so the field holds the value 0x01. The second byte is the packet type and the third is a type modifier. The modifiers are only meaningful in the context of their type, and the memo uses the notation type[modifier], so data[eow] is a data packet with the end of window modifier set. The fourth byte is the client's subchannel value, whose meaning is defined by the transport client and which therefore applies only to data packets; all other packet types must carry zero there.

Next come two 32-bit connection identifiers. The source connection identifier is a value unique to the transmitting transport, assigned when the transport is created, and it is part of the transport address. The destination connection identifier is the 32-bit identifier of the target transport, and it comes in three kinds: the unknown identifier, whose value is 0x00000000 and which is used only in a join request; the multicast identifier, which the master hands over in the join confirmation and which is used with the multicast network address to form the destination address of every packet sent to the whole web; and a unicast identifier, one per member, used for packets sent to that member alone.

The message acceptance criteria is a multiple part record. Its most significant 8 bits are a flag that, if not zero, says synchronisation is required; the default is that no synchronisation is required. The rest is a 12-element vector holding the status of the last 12 messages, two bits each, with the values accepted, pending and rejected. Only the master may set message status, and the master may not shift a pending status out of the end of the vector. Message sequence numbers are 16-bit unsigned values that the master initialises to zero and increments by one for each token granted; packet sequence numbers are 16-bit unsigned numbers that the producing process assigns per message, starting at zero.

The last three fields are the parameters that shape the transport. Heartbeat is a 32-bit unsigned number of milliseconds, shared by every member of the web, and by definition at least one packet is multicast into the web during every heartbeat period. Window is a 16-bit unsigned number giving the maximum number of data packets a member may multicast in one heartbeat, counting retransmitted and new packets together. Retention is a 16-bit unsigned number of heartbeats for which a producer must keep its transmitted data and state in case it has to be retransmitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Every MTP packet starts with the same fixed header. It says which version of the protocol this is, what kind of packet it is, who sent it, who should get it, how the group agrees on which messages arrived, and the three numbers that set the pace of the whole web.

sections.title: Joining a Web and Being Given a Token
sections.content:
Before any meeting can happen a process must acquire a network service access point, the address of the machine where the service is available. The process that establishes that address first becomes the master of the web. Which process takes that role has to be decided in advance, so that creation is unambiguous even when the network is partitioned. The new master should make a robust effort to check that the address is not already in service, which it can do by repeatedly sending join requests to the web's unknown transport address; if there is no answer it may be fairly confident the address is free, and if there is an answer the creation must be abandoned and the situation reported to its client.

Further members join by sending a join request to the unknown address. The request must have zeros in all of the acceptance fields, and its data carries the parameters the client has asked for. The membership class is master, producer or consumer. The transport class is reliable, which generates and processes negative acknowledgements so that data is delivered or the failure is detected and reported, or unreliable, which offers best effort delivery and tolerates loss or corruption. The transport type is NxN, where several producers are accepted, or 1xN, where only a single producer whose identity was fixed in advance is allowed.

The client also states its minimum acceptable throughput in kilobytes per second, calculated from the heartbeat, window and maximum data unit size rather than from measured traffic, and may suggest a maximum data unit size in bytes. Only the master answers a join request, with either a confirmation or a denial; a denial may be because the new member asked for parameters that conflict with those already set. The confirmation is unicast and carries the web's current operating parameters, which the joining member must then accept as the values in force. The master must hold all the transmit tokens when it sends a confirmation, so that a new member sees only complete messages.

Before any process may transmit client data or state it must hold a transmit token. It asks for one by sending a token request unicast to the master, retransmitting at intervals of about one heartbeat. The master may apply fairness rules, and at a minimum should queue requests first in, first out, ignoring duplicate requests from the same member and keeping the first unhonoured one. When the master grants a token it unicasts a token confirmation, whose data field lists all the multicast addresses of the networks currently represented in the web.

The master tracks each token in one of three states: idle, when it is not assigned; pending, when it has been assigned but the master has not yet seen any data carrying the assigned message number; and busy, when it has been assigned and data has arrived but the message is still in the acceptance vector. If the master detects no data and no heartbeat from a token holder it assumes the token is lost, tries to confirm the process is still there, and if there is no answer removes it from the web, marks the message rejected and takes the token back itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The first program to claim an address becomes the chair of the group. Others ask to join and say what they need; the chair either agrees and tells them the group's settings, or refuses. Nobody may send anything until the chair hands out a token, and the chair gives out one at a time.

sections.title: Sending Data and Getting It Back
sections.content:
Client data arrives as uninterpreted bytes, which are put straight after the fixed header fields. A packet may carry any number of data bytes, from zero up to the maximum size of a network packet less the network and transport overhead. Every packet that consumes a sequence number must contain either client data or a client state transition such as an end of message or a subchannel change. Packets go out in bursts called windows, and the protocol guarantees that no more than the current window value of data packets is multicast by a single process during one heartbeat. Every packet carries the latest heartbeat, window and retention values.

When there is not enough client data to fill a packet, an empty dally packet is multicast instead, to keep the web synchronised and to advertise the producer's highest sequence number. A message should consist of several packets so that consumers are likely to see at least one of them and so identify the producer, which means a message must consist of at least retention packets, with empty dally packets appended when the client's data does not fill that many. A producer holding a token with nothing to send multicasts an empty cancel packet, handing the token back to the master, which then marks the message rejected so that other consumers do not try to recover it. When the web is idle the master may send empty hibernate packets at a much slower rate than the heartbeat to cut network traffic.

Loss is detected in two ways: by receiving a data or heartbeat packet with a sequence number higher than expected from that producer, or by receiving a fragment with no end of message and then nothing more from that producer for more than a single heartbeat. The consumer then sends a negative acknowledgement, unicast to the producer, whose data field lists the ascending pairs of sequence numbers needed to recover what was missed. A producer that can no longer retransmit what was asked for answers with a nak denial, and if that leaves the consumer in a failed state the consumer withdraws from the web. Packets that are retransmitted are multicast to the whole web again, carrying the original client information and the original sequence numbers but updated parameter values, and they have priority over new data. Because retransmissions count against the window, less new data can go out in that heartbeat. Consumers must be prepared to ignore duplicate packets, which are the inevitable result of one consumer's request being answered to everyone.

Operations are retried so that a single lost packet does not fail the transport: the interval between retries is the heartbeat, and the number of retries is retention. The retriable operations are join, nak, token, isMember and quit. A process that sees another member breaking the protocol may ask it to withdraw by unicasting a quit request at it.
sections.plainLanguage: Data goes out to everyone as a burst of packets, and the receiver stays quiet when it arrives. If something is missing, the receiver says so, privately, and the sender sends that piece again to the whole group. If a member breaks the rules, another member can ask it to leave.

sections.title: Choosing Heartbeat, Window and Retention
sections.content:
The memo gives worked numbers for the three parameters rather than leaving them to guesswork. The heartbeat is approximately the transport time constant. The example assumes a one MIP processor on Ethernet with an industry standard disk, where the worst case page fault resolution needing two seeks at an average seek time of 40 milliseconds should be under 80 milliseconds; twice that is taken as the minimum sensible time constant, giving a heartbeat of 160 to 200 milliseconds. The transmit time for a full Ethernet packet is about 1.2 milliseconds and processing under 3 milliseconds, so a packet takes about 8.4 milliseconds and the theoretical maximum is about 17 packets per heartbeat, or 120 packets a second, which sets a window of 17 to 20 packets per heartbeat and a theoretical throughput of 180 kilobytes per second.

Retention is the third number. Over a local network, data lost to corruption on the data link should be around one packet in every 50,000, a bit error rate of approximately 10 to the power of minus nine, and telephony links between routers are similar. Far more packets are lost in the switches than on the physical links, usually through congestion and resource starvation, and that kind of loss is virtually unavoidable. Since a receiver cannot send a negative acknowledgement until the following heartbeat, and the acknowledgement should have the chance to be sent at least twice, the minimum retention is 3. The resources committed to a producer on these assumptions are buffers for 80 packets of 1500 bytes each, with each buffer committed for 600 to 800 milliseconds.

Transports that span more than one network have their own problem. If a router drops a packet, every process on the far side may send a negative acknowledgement at the same time, which will not improve the router's service, and one request is enough to prompt the producer to retransmit. The suggested remedy is to raise the minimum retention to a value N and then use a randomising function that returns a value between zero and N minus 2 to choose how many heartbeat intervals to wait before sending the request, spreading the requests out in time. For internet cases the minimum retention is therefore 5.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does the arithmetic for you. It works out that a heartbeat of about 160 to 200 milliseconds, a window of 17 to 20 packets and a retention of 3 heartbeats give a reliable transport on a local network, and that a retention of 5 is safer when the web spans the internet, because the acknowledgements then arrive at different moments instead of all at once.

sections.title: Running MTP over the Internet
sections.content:
The appendix works out how to carry MTP over Internet Protocol. A transport needs two things from the network below it: a way of addressing processes within a machine, ports or sockets, and a mechanism for multicast addressing of datagrams. MTP on IP uses the IP multicast mechanisms defined in RFC 1112 and requires Level 2 conformance from hosts that both send and receive multicast packets, on the local network and on the internet. It uses the permanent host group address 224.0.1.9.

IP has no port mechanism of its own, since ports belong to the transport layer, so the memo defines a simple bridge protocol that runs on top of IP and carries one MTP packet per bridge packet. The IP protocol field carries the value 92 decimal to say that the payload is MTP. The bridge header has a destination port, a source port, a length and a checksum, followed by the data. The length counts the octets of the bridged packet, header and all data, with a minimum of 8 and a maximum of 65535, and does not include padding bytes used for the checksum. The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the whole bridge header and data, padded with a zero octet if needed to make multiple 16-bit quantities; a computed checksum of all zeros is changed to all ones, and the field is optional, with all zeros meaning that checksums are not in use.

The memo notes that the bridge protocol looks much like the User Datagram Protocol, and says why UDP itself was not used: the protocol field in the IP packet should show that the protocol of interest is MTP.

The Security Considerations section is one line: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: To run MTP over the internet the memo adds a small bridge protocol that carries one MTP packet per IP packet, and it uses the IP multicast group address 224.0.1.9. The bridge looks like UDP but has its own IP protocol number, so that receivers can tell the difference.

fields.name: Protocol Version
fields.desc: Version 1 of MTP uses the value 0x01.

fields.name: Packet Type
fields.desc: data, nak, empty, join, quit, token or isMember.

fields.name: Type Modifier
fields.desc: Refines the packet type, for example data with eow or eom.

fields.name: Client Channel
fields.desc: The client's subchannel value; zero for every packet type other than data.

fields.name: Source Connection Identifier
fields.desc: A value unique to the transmitting transport, assigned when the transport is created.

fields.name: Destination Connection Identifier
fields.desc: The target transport: unknown, multicast or unicast.

fields.name: Message Acceptance Criteria
fields.desc: A synchronisation flag and a 12-element vector holding the status of the last 12 messages.

fields.name: Heartbeat
fields.desc: The shared interval in milliseconds; at least one packet is multicast per heartbeat.

fields.name: Window
fields.desc: The maximum number of data packets a member may multicast in one heartbeat.

fields.name: Retention
fields.desc: The number of heartbeats a producer must retain data for retransmission.

items.label: data
items.desc: Carries user information; only the holder of a transmit token may send it, and all data packets are multicast to the whole web.

items.label: nak
items.desc: A consumer asks for retransmission of missing packets, or the producer denies that it can still retransmit them. Always unicast.

items.label: empty
items.desc: Multicast when there is no client data: dally to keep synchronisation, cancel to hand back a token, hibernate when the web is idle.

items.label: join
items.desc: A request to join the web, and the master's confirmation or denial of it.

items.label: quit
items.desc: A request to leave the web, and the confirmation that it has been observed.

items.label: token
items.desc: A producer's request for permission to transmit, and the master's grant of it.

items.label: isMember
items.desc: A check that a given process is a recognised member of the web.

viz.caption: THE JOIN AND TOKEN EXCHANGE DESCRIBED IN RFC 1301

messages.label: JOIN[REQUEST]
messages.note: Sent to the web's unknown address with the membership class, transport class and transport type the client asked for.

messages.label: JOIN[CONFIRM]
messages.note: The master unicasts the web's operating parameters and the multicast connection identifier.

messages.label: TOKEN[REQUEST]
messages.note: A producer asks the master for permission to send.

messages.label: TOKEN[CONFIRM]
messages.note: The master grants the token, which carries the message sequence number.

messages.label: DATA
messages.note: Data packets are multicast to the entire web.

messages.label: NAK[REQUEST]
messages.note: A consumer that missed a packet asks for it back, unicast to the producer.
